stories.title: CM Himanta Biswa Sarma Leaves for Delhi to Brief PM Modi on Assam Floods
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Guwahati: Chief Minister Dr Himanta Biswa Sarma left for New Delhi today for a few days' visit.
He is scheduled to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi during his visit.
Sources said the CM is supposed to brief PM Modi on the current flood situation in the state.
It needs to be mentioned here that Union Minister JP Nadda had visited Upper Assam during the floods, as well as an inter-ministerial central team, to assess the damages.
Until this morning, the death toll in the recent devastating floods stood at 105.
Water is still present in some villages, exactly one month after a sudden deluge struck the Upper Assam districts of Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat and Golaghat on July 19.

stories.headline: Israeli strikes hit an air base hours after a Turkish delegation visit, Syrian officials say
stories.title: Israeli strikes hit an air base hours after a Turkish delegation visit, Syrian officials say
stories.summary: Damascus, Aug 19: A Turkish delegation had visited an air base in northern Syria the day before it was hit by Israeli airstrikes, Syrian officials said. The Israeli strikes hit the Abu Duhur base early Tuesday, hours after the delegation had left, causing damage but no casualties. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said in a statement that Israel had attacked the base because Syria was “on the verge of breaching” an agreed-upon “status quo in security matters” by allowing Turkish troops to deploy there. Two Syrian officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly said the Turkish delegation had visited the air base in the northwestern province of Idlib on Monday to review rehabilitation work underway at the facility. It was the first confirmation of a Turkish presence at the Abu Duhur base. Turkish and Syrian officials have not publicly commented on Turkiye's role there but have condemned the attack, as did Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkiye who also serves as special envoy to Syria, and a number of Arab countries. Turkish officials on Wednesday did not comment on the reported presence of a Turkish military delegation. But Turkiye's communications directorate accused Netanyahu of making “untenable allegations ... intended to legitimize Israel's unlawful airstrikes targeting Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity.” It alleged that Netanyahu aimed “to pursue expansionist and destabilizing policies in the region ahead of the elections in Israel.” Turkiye “will resolutely continue to cooperate with the Syrian Government on a legitimate basis for the establishment of peace, stability, and prosperity in Syria, and will never allow the destabilization of Syria,” it said. The Abu Duhur air base lies at a strategic location near the borders between Idlib, Aleppo and Hama provinces. During the time of former Syrian President Bashar Assad, who was ousted by a rebel offensive in December 2024, MiG-23 and MiG-21 fighter jets and L-39 aircraft operated out of the base. Turkiye has been supporting Syria's effort to rebuild its armed forces by training Syrian personnel at Turkish military schools and bases, and by supplying equipment and logistical support. Officials have not disclosed the types of equipment involved. The two countries signed an agreement last year that formalized their military cooperation. Earlier this year, Syrian troops also took part in military exercises held in Turkiye. Turkish officials have repeatedly stated that Ankara does not consider Syria's security separate from its own. Israel, meanwhile, has remained suspicious of the new authorities in Damascus, led by former Islamist insurgents. Syria's interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa has said repeatedly that he does not want a conflict with Israel. Israel carried out hundreds of airstrikes around Syria after Assad's fall, mainly destroying assets of the Syrian army to keep them out of the hands of his successors. The Israeli military also seized control of a U.N.-patrolled buffer zone in southern Syria, which it continues to occupy. The Israeli army's chief of staff, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, on Wednesday toured the occupied area in Syria and told troops, “We will not allow hostile forces to establish themselves on our borders, and we will know how to use our operational capabilities precisely where and when needed.” Turkiye, a NATO member that also recently signed a defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, gave no indication that it would respond militarily to the Israeli strikes in Syria, but the incident added further strain to already tense Turkish-Israeli relations. Turkiye and Israel once were close allies, but the relationship has been marked by deep frictions under Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's more than two-decade rule, despite brief periods of reconciliation. Erdogan is an outspoken critic of Israel's policies toward the Palestinians, while Israel has been angered by Erdogan's support for the Hamas militant group. The fall of Assad's government further strained their relations as the two rivals sought to curb each other's influence in the neighboring country, with some analysts fearing that they could be headed toward a proxy war.

stories.headline: Christianity & Kashmir: A Shared Legacy
stories.title: Christianity & Kashmir: A Shared Legacy
stories.summary: Christianity and Kashmir have a shared legacy as Christian missionaries have played a pivotal role in laying the foundation of education system in this beautiful land that left a lasting imprint on its social and intellectual development. Roots of the Christian educators can be traced back to late 19th century when they introduced the concept of structured schooling, modern subjects, physical training and girls’ education in the Valley.Classrooms of the missionary schools brought together children from different communities. These institutions became spaces where education, friendship, sport, discipline and shared experiences often transcended religious boundaries. Long before phrases such as interfaith dialogue and social cohesion became part of public vocabulary, generations of Kashmiris experienced diversity naturally inside these institutions. Across Kashmir, former students of Christian missionary schools became doctors, engineers,administrators, politicians, religious leaders, diplomats, academics, entrepreneurs, journalists,lawyers, artists, industrialists, hoteliers and public servants. Some remained in Kashmir. Others carried their education across India and around the world. Stories of these students form an important part of Kashmir’s modern social history and drive home a point that a school can have a religious identity and still make an educational contribution to a society much larger than that religious community. TYNDALE BISCOE SCHOOL A significant milestone in the educational history of Kashmir came in 1880, when the Church Mission Society established a school in Srinagar under Reverend J. Hinton Knowles. The institution gradually developed into the educational tradition associated with Tyndale Biscoe. Canon Cecil Tyndale-Biscoe, who joined the school in the 1890s, left a lasting imprint through his emphasis on discipline, physical education, self-reliance, service and character. Its alumni reflect the remarkable diversity. They include Dr Farooq Abdullah, former Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir; Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi, Member of Parliament from Srinagar; Moulvi Imran Raza Ansari, prominent Shia cleric and political leader; Dr Anil Bhan, renowned cardiac surgeon and P. N. Dhar, economist and former senior adviser to Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The institution’s alumni also include first IAS topper from J&K, Shah Faesal. MALLINSON GIRLS’ SCHOOL Mallinson Girls’ School was established in October 1912 by Miss Violet B. Fitze as the Girls’ Mission High School, initially operating from a modest mud house at Fateh Kadal in Srinagar’s old city. Fitze, a missionary educator, founded the institution under the auspices of the Church Missionary Society (CMS), marking it as a dedicated effort to introduce formal schooling for girls in the region. In the mid-20th century, the CMS Girls School at Fateh Kadal in Srinagar, faced increasing enrolment and spatial constraints due to its rapid growth under missionary leadership. By the late 1950s, the decision was made to relocate the institution to a more expansive site near Lal Chowk area. The move was completed in 1962, coinciding with the retirement of principal Miss Muriel P. Mallinson after her 40-year tenure from 1922 to 1962, and positioned the school adjacent to the CMS Boys’ School (now Tyndale Biscoe School), facilitating shared infrastructure on a donated plot that supported further development. ST JOSEPH’S SCHOOL BARAMULLA Another important institution St Joseph’s Higher Secondary School Baramulla in North Kashmir was established by the Mill Hill Fathers or Mill Hill Missionaries from London in 1903 for everyone without any distinction of religion, caste, creed or colour. It was run by Society of Jesus after Mill Hill Missionaries left the mission. Among its distinguished alumni was Dr Mohammad Najibullah, who later became President of Afghanistan. His journey from a school in Baramulla to the presidency of Afghanistan is a remarkable example of how far the influence of a Kashmiri educational institution could travel. The school’s alumni also include figures former minister and a senior politician Syed Altaf Bukhari, former bureaucrat Muhammad Ashraf Bukhari and others. PRESENTATION CONVENT The Presentation Convent was founded in 1936 by Sisters Peter Conway, Sacred Heart, Annunciata, and Xavier—who relocated from Rawalpindi at the invitation of Maharaja Hari Singh—the school commenced operations in Srinagar before shifting to its current 10-acre site at Rajbagh in Srinagar along the Jhelum River in 1939, with initial government support for land lease and construction. In 1977 it transitioned to an exclusively girls’ day school emphasizing value-based instruction, life skills, critical thinking, and alignment with principles of tolerance and inclusivity, guided by the motto “Virtue and Labour.” Among those associated with its alumni tradition are Mehbooba Mufti, former Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir; Nilofer Khan, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Kashmir; late Aasiya Jeelani, journalist and human-rights activist. BURN HALL SCHOOL Burn Hall School in Srinagar, Kashmir, was established in 1942 by the Mill Hill Missionaries, specifically by Fathers Tijssen and S. De Jong. The school was initially started as the Senior Cambridge School. The school closed down temporarily following the Pakistani invasion that occurred during the India-Pakistan War of 1947–1948. The school was restarted by Fr. J. Boerkamp in 1956 as the founding father and the first principal of the school he rendered yeomen service to the cause of education in the valley. The school became part of the wider Mill Hill missionary educational tradition. In 1976 tragedy struck the Burn Hall School in the form of a major fire that engulfed the building on March 27. The school was completely gutted down. After fairly protracted negotiations with Misereor of Germany and Cebemo of the Netherlands, financial support came in, and the school was rebuilt. The new Burn Hall complex was inaugurated by lateSheikh Mohammad Abdullah, then Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir, on 20 September 1978. That moment was significant in its own right. A Christian educational institution had become so deeply embedded in Kashmir’s social landscape that its new complex was inaugurated by one of the Valley’s most powerful political leaders. BURN HALL ALUMNI LEGACY Burn Hall over the decades has produced an unusually diverse body of alumni who have contributed to politics, public administration, diplomacy, academia, business, literature, journalism, the arts and other professions. Among its most prominent alumni is Omar Abdullah, presently the Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir. His journey from the classrooms of Burn Hall to the highest elected political office in the Union Territory is an important part of the institution’s contemporary legacy. Another distinguished alumnus is Vikram Misri, Foreign Secretary of India, whose diplomatic career has included serving as India’s Ambassador to China, Spain and Myanmar and as Deputy National Security Adviser. His journey from a Srinagar school to one of the country’s highest diplomatic positions is a remarkable example of the reach of education. The alumni story also includes Haseeb Drabu, economist, former Finance Minister of Jammu and Kashmir and former Chairman of Jammu & Kashmir Bank; Agha Shahid Ali, the internationally acclaimed poet; Rohit Bal, one of India’s best-known fashion designers. Among its political alumni are Tanvir Sadiq and Lone brothers, while the wider alumni community has made its mark in medicine, civil administration, academia, business, journalism and cinema. Perhaps one of the most striking names in this story is Mirwaiz-e-Kashmir, Molvi Umar Farooq. His association with Burn Hall offers a particularly powerful illustration of Kashmir’s plural educational tradition. A future Muslim religious leader received part of his formative education in a Christian institution. There is no contradiction in that history. Rather, it demonstrates how education can create common spaces without requiring people to surrender their individual faiths or identities. The school’s historical material also records my name among its notable alumni. My own journey did not end when I left the school gates. In 1995, I was elected President of the Students’ Union. During that period, I became closely engaged with students’ concerns, their rights and wider human rights issues. That experience became an important formative chapter in my public life. It gave me an opportunity to engage directly with young people, understand their aspirations and concerns, and appreciate the importance of giving a voice to those who often feel unheard. Looking back, I see that experience as part of the wider confidence, discipline and sense of civic responsibility that education helped cultivate in me. And among the political alumni are the Lone brothers, whose association with Burn Hall adds yet another dimension to the institution’s long and diverse public legacy. PERSONAL CONNECTION I write about this legacy with a deeply personal connection. I am a Kashmiri Muslim and an alumnus of Burn Hall School. My wife is a practising Christian from South India who has made Kashmir her home and has worked in a senior administrative and human resources role at a missionary school in Srinagar. Both my daughters have also received their high-school education at Presentation Convent School in Srinagar. For our family, therefore, Christian education in Kashmir is not simply a subject of history. It is part of our lived experience. I experienced it as a student. My wife has experienced it as a Christian professional working within the educational tradition. My daughters have experienced it as students. Our association with interfaith engagement has also extended beyond Kashmir. My wife and I have been associated with US-based interfaith organisations and initiatives that promote dialogue, understanding and cooperation among people of different faiths. Those experiences have reinforced a simple belief: interfaith harmony does not require us to erase our differences. It requires us to respect those differences while finding common ground. In our own home, this understanding is lived rather than merely discussed. We celebrate Eid and Christmas together, sharing in each other’s traditions with respect and affection. For us, this does not diminish either faith. It reflects something more fundamental — family, love, friendship and mutual respect. Sheikh Khalid Jehangir is Director of the International Centre for Peace Studies (ICPS), former Vice Chairman of JKPCC, and the BJP’s 2019 Lok Sabha candidate from Srinagar. He is a regular columnist for Greater Kashmir, has worked with national and international news organizations, and has authored books on Kashmir.

stories.headline: Getting it right, not getting it wrong
stories.title: Getting it right, not getting it wrong
stories.summary: When a contractor’s Input Tax Credit worth over ten crores goes silent overnight, the taxpayer feels the shock first. But behind every Rule 86A action lies a department that has, at some point, formed a considered view that revenue is at risk — from fake invoicing, circular trading, or credit claimed without any underlying supply. The Hon’ble High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at Srinagar, vide judgment dated 12.08.2026 in NCC Limited [WP(C) 1935/2026], set aside the departmental communication blocking Input Tax Credit (ITC) of ₹10,45,38,432/-. Read quickly, this can look like a setback for the department. Read properly, it is nothing of the kind — it is the Court doing exactly what judiciary should do: telling the department how to make its orders and actions bullet proof, rather than telling it to stop enforcing. The power itself was never in doubt The most important line in the entire order is easy to miss because it comes almost as an afterthought: the Bench expressly clarified that setting aside the communication “shall not come in the way of the Competent Authority... to pass an appropriate order under Rule 86-A... after providing the petitioner an adequate opportunity of being heard.” Read that again. The Court did not say the department was wrong to suspect the credit. It did not say Rs. 10.45 crore was safe. It did not restore the credit to NCC Limited’s ledger without conditions. It simply sent the case back with an instruction: do it again, and do it with reasons on record and a hearing given. That is not a defeat for the department — it is a second chance to issue an order that will actually survive scrutiny at every subsequent stage, from appeal to Tribunal to writ court. This matters because an order that is set aside on a technical or procedural ground is an order the department gets to correct. An order that survives on a weak procedural foundation but is later challenged on merits, after years of litigation, is a far costlier outcome for revenue. The NCC Limited Judgement should be read by every GST Officer as a warning against the wrong kind of risk — not the risk of blocking bogus credit, but the risk of handing the taxpayer an easy exit route on a paperwork lapse. A useful discipline, not a new burden Rule 86A already required “reasons to believe,” recorded in writing, before any blocking order could be passed. That requirement was never optional; it was built into the rule from the outset precisely so that the power would be used with rigour and not casually. What the J&K High Court has done — following the Karnataka High Court in K-9 Enterprises (whose SLP the Supreme Court dismissed) and the Telangana High Court in Bhavani Oxides — is read a further, closely related discipline into the same provision: a short opportunity of hearing before the block, given how adversely it affects the taxpayer’s cash flow and business operations. Far from weakening the department’s hand, this discipline strengthens it. A blocking order preceded by even a brief notice, and grounded in specific, recorded reasons — mismatches in GSTR-2B, absence of proof of actual receipt of goods, non-existent or non-functional suppliers, values inconsistent with e-way bill trails — becomes far harder for any taxpayer’s counsel to dislodge on appeal. It converts a suspicion into a documented finding. Officers who already build their Rule 86A cases this way — recording the specific red flags, will find that this judgment changes nothing about how they already work. It simply makes explicit the standard the best GST cases were always meeting. What this means going forward For GST Officers, the message from NCC Limited Judgement is not caution but confidence: use Rule 86A firmly against every genuine case of fraudulent or ineligible credit, but build the case the way the law always intended — reasons recorded before the order is signed, a short notice or hearing given wherever the urgency of the situation allows it, and the blocked quantum tied transparently to the credit balance actually standing in the ledger. Orders built this way do not get set aside; they get upheld, and they send the clearest possible signal to habitual evaders that the department’s enforcement machinery is both vigorous and legally unassailable. The department’s interest is never served by a shortcut. It is served by a Rule 86A order that a taxpayer’s lawyer reads and decides not to challenge at all. (The author is a State Taxes Officer posted at Circle-C, Srinagar. Views are personal.)

stories.headline: CERC's Price Cap Could be A Brake Energy Storage Can Do without In India
stories.title: CERC's Price Cap Could be A Brake Energy Storage Can Do without In India
stories.summary: India's power exchanges cap spot prices at ₹10 per unit, a number that has moved around (₹20, then ₹12 , now ₹10) every time the regulator (CERC) has judged the market too hot to be trusted. The logic each time has been consumer protection: don't let scarcity turn into extortion. But the same regulator has quietly admitted the cap doesn't hold for gas and imported coal. When gas and imported-coal plants can't cover their costs at ₹10, they're waved into a separate High Price Day-Ahead Market ( HP-DAM ) with no ceiling at all for high cost generators. In April 2026, HP-DAM cleared at an average of ₹19.6 per unit — nearly double the official ceiling even as the capped DAM segment traded at just ₹5.3. The system has, in effect, built an escape hatch for the most expensive, higher polluting power on the grid, and left the technology built to replace it stuck outside. The petition on CERC's desk That technology's advocates have taken the argument to the regulator directly. The National Solar Energy Federation of India (NSEFI) filed Petition No. 60/MP/2026 in November 2025, asking the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission to scrap the ₹10/kWh bid ceiling altogether across every market segment- Day-Ahead, Real-Time, Term-Ahead, all of it or, failing that, to raise it to ₹15/kWh. The petition names Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and Pumped Storage Projects (PSP) specifically as the technologies being squeezed. Since it was first heard in Feb 2026, no order has been issued. DATE WHAT HAPPENED SHAPE \* MERGEFORMAT NSEFI's core argument is about the shape of storage revenue, not its existence. A battery earns nothing while it charges and everything in the two or three hours it discharges into the evening peak. That spread is the entire business model. Cap the peak price and the spread collapses, no matter how cheap the midday charging power gets. Producers, the petition says, are "forced to sell power at low prices during weak demand periods" but the ceiling prevents them from "recovering those losses when demand rises." And the HP-DAM escape hatch that was supposed to fix this hasn't worked as a fix for storage either. NSEFI's filing says the segment has seen "limited activity because there are few buyers willing to purchase electricity at those rates," since debt-laden DISCOMs would rather load-shed than pay premium spot prices. Storage should be rewarded for speed, not penalised for it There's a case that the cap actually inverts the incentive it should be creating. Gas peakers need real lead time with even the fastest aero-derivative turbines taking several minutes to sync and ramp, and open-cycle gas turbines typically need 10–15 minutes from a cold start. Batteries respond in milliseconds: grid-scale BESS installations detect a frequency deviation and inject power in well under a second, an order of magnitude faster than anything gas can offer. A market designed around scarcity value should, in theory, pay the fastest, most controllable resource the most for showing up at the moment of stress, not cap its main revenue stream while carving out an uncapped side-market for the slower, dirtier alternative. In effect, a regulator that guarantees storage a 14% return with one hand is capping the only revenue stream that lets it earn that return with the other. That tension runs right through CERC's own recent decisions. In March 2026 the Commission finalised a tariff framework for storage bundled with thermal or transmission assets, guaranteeing a 14% return on equity and setting minimum round-trip-efficiency standards, in a clear vote of confidence in storage as an asset class. But that framework only helps regulated, contracted storage. It does nothing for merchant storage trying to earn its keep on the open exchange, which is exactly the model India leaned on in 2025 when it awarded a record 10.4 GW of standalone BESS capacity, much of it at tariffs competitive bidding has already pushed close to the edge of viability. It is also a key reason even large developers from Adani Green to Acme to ReNew continue to seek long term PPAs for their storage installations, looking at merchant sales only ass a stop gap opportunity to get better value for their investmemnts. How other markets price scarcity Every functioning power market caps prices somewhere. The debate is never whether to cap, but where, and how the cap interacts with battery economics. Placed side by side, India's ceiling stands out for how conservative it is relative to peers that also run energy-only markets, we have considered Texas's ERCOT prices and Australia, as both have well established power trading markets like India. SHAPE \* MERGEFORMAT Texas's ERCOT, an energy-only market with no separate capacity mechanism, caps prices at $5,000/MWh — roughly forty times India's ceiling, precisely because scarcity pricing is the only signal ERCOT gives generators and batteries to build. Australia's NEM is more instructive still: the Australian Energy Market Commission is in the middle of a deliberate, multi-year step-up of its Market Price Cap, rising to A$23,200/MWh from 1 July 2026, specifically because its own analysis found the prior cap was "too low to ensure there is enough generation and battery storage to keep the system reliable." That is the same argument NSEFI makes, already accepted and acted on by a peer regulator. What could change A few things are moving at once, and any one of them could reshape this argument before CERC rules on NSEFI's petition: ● A blanket cap increase (to ₹15, as NSEFI's fallback ask, or higher) would help storage and gas/imported-coal alike — raising DISCOM exposure to fossil peakers along with it, which is the political sensitivity that has kept the cap low in the first place. ● A storage-specific carve-out. A wider trading band only for BESS/pumped-storage discharge would target the incentive without reopening the door to broader fossil-peaker profiteering, though it would add another layer of complexity to an already segmented market (DAM, HP-DAM, RTM, G-DAM). ● Market coupling, being rolled out in phases from January 2026 and currently contested by IEX at the Supreme Court, will pool bids across all exchanges into a single clearing price could be a structural change to price discovery that could matter as much to storage revenue as the cap itself, independent of how CERC rules on the ₹10 question. For now, the order on the NSEFI petition remains reserved. One wonders how much extra storage coiuld have been added with a favourable decision, or even the added urgency to those plans.

stories.headline: India’s defensive cracks threaten Hockey World Cup title bid despite Pakistan win
stories.title: India’s defensive cracks threaten Hockey World Cup title bid despite Pakistan win
stories.summary: India beat Pakistan 5-3 to enter the World Cup hockey second round, but a leaky defence and repeated errors raise doubts over its title credentials against Netherlands and Argentina.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'world cup' in title weight 42
event term: 'world cup' in summary weight 25.2
article_sentences: There is no real away World Cup if you are an Indian team.
You will be hard-pressed to go to a corner of the globe without running into an Indian.
Amstelveen, one of the co-hosts of the World Cup, is no exception.
The suburb south of Amsterdam is home to more Indians than any other nationality.

For skipper Harmanpreet Singh, the game against Pakistan felt like ‘playing in India.’ After his two goals in the 5-3 win on Wednesday, which took him to the top of the goal charts, Harmanpreet was rightly serenaded by the Indian supporters, who had turned out in large numbers to show their love.
But with admiration also comes the pressure to perform.
There are expectations for India to return to the podium after 51 years, with a yearning to reclaim the crown.
Yet despite two wins in three matches and securing qualification to the second round, India has underwhelmed.

The eight goals conceded (third-worst defensive record among the 16 teams), the drop in intensity, and the lack of control exhibited while defending leads hardly make India look like a credible title challenger.
India has played only one of the tournament’s top sides so far.
Its next opponents, Netherlands and possibly Argentina, will not extend that courtesy.
India lost heavily in its two Pro League home games against the South American team and came out with a win and a loss against Netherlands in Rotterdam.
